name: Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica
summary:
The Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica of Ottawa (Basilique-cathédrale Notre-Dame d'Ottawa) is Canada's oldest and most historically significant Roman Catholic cathedral, built between 1839 and 1885 CE and designated a National Historic Site of Canada. It stands at the heart of Ottawa, overlooking Parliament Hill, and was the primary Catholic cathedral during the formation of the Canadian Confederation (1867) — its Gothic Revival twin spires rising beside the Parliament buildings that shaped the symbolic landscape of Canada's capital.

The cathedral was built on land set aside by Colonel By, founder of Bytown (now Ottawa), during the construction of the Rideau Canal. Father Joseph-Bruno Guigues, the first Bishop of Ottawa, oversaw the early construction, which was completed over decades. The twin towers, completed in 1858 and 1890, were designed to visually counterbalance Parliament's Centre Block across the Ottawa River, creating the distinctive Ottawa skyline that frames Canadian federal power between church and state.

The cathedral houses the famous 1894-1895 pipe organ by Casavant Frères — one of Canada's finest historic instruments — and contains decorative programs reflecting French-Canadian Catholic heritage in the capital. The cathedral's presence beside Parliament Hill, where the French-Canadian Catholic community's national cathedral stands alongside English Protestant governmental buildings, encapsulates the bilingual, bicultural tension and compromise at the heart of Canadian confederation.
